name: Axonal Stretch Resonance Lance
description:
The Axonal Stretch Resonance Lance generates a low-frequency oscillating traction field through a pair of piezoelectric transducer arrays mounted along its barrel. The field, when sustained against a target, induces rapid cyclical mechanical deformation in long axonal fibers — particularly those in peripheral motor nerves and the spinal cord's dorsal columns. The effect is analogous to diffuse axonal injury produced by high-velocity trauma, but delivered remotely, gradually, and with a degree of anatomical targeting determined by the operator's aim point.

The ASRL-3 is most often aimed at the spine or upper limbs. Sustained fire on the cervical spine produces ascending paralysis beginning in the fingers and progressing toward the diaphragm over thirty to ninety seconds. Aimed at a limb, it produces first a violent involuntary tremor, then loss of fine motor control, then gross motor failure, as progressively larger axon populations are disrupted. The tremor phase — which operators call 'the twitch' and which gave the weapon its street name — is visually distinctive and deeply unsettling to witnesses, which has made the ASRL-3 a preferred intimidation instrument in certain criminal contexts.

Zheng-Dao Bioelectric's development documentation describes the ASRL-3 as an 'axonal conduction research platform' and its field versions as unauthorized derivatives. This position is legally convenient but widely disbelieved; the field version's ergonomics, power management system, and targeting reticle are clearly purpose-built for operator use, not laboratory work. Recovery from ASRL-3 exposure depends heavily on the duration of field contact: brief exposures resolve within hours, while sustained exposures of fifteen seconds or more to major nerve trunks may result in permanent conduction deficits.
legality: Restricted — prohibited for civilian ownership, licensed for specific research and security applications
specifications:
effective range: 35 meters
field oscillation frequency: Adjustable 8–22 Hz
time to motor disruption: 4–8 seconds at optimal frequency match
time to incapacitation: 15–30 seconds sustained
weight: 5.3 kg
power draw: High — 8 shots per standard cell at full duration
targeting aid: Anatomical zone reticle overlay with nerve trunk markers
recovery window: Under 5 seconds: full recovery likely. 5–15 seconds: hours to days. Over 15 seconds: permanent damage possible
tactical_use: Operators use the ASRL-3 for target incapacitation where the tremor display serves a dual purpose: the target is disabled and bystanders are deterred. In extraction operations, it is used to disable a target's weapon arm without killing. Criminal enforcers use brief exposures as a punishment tool — enough to cause the tremor and short-term motor loss, but not enough to create permanent damage that would attract medical attention. Anti-cyberware note: synthetic limb replacements are unaffected, but the biological nerve trunks interfacing with implants remain vulnerable.
cultural_context: The ASRL-3 has a particularly grim reputation in GLMZ's labor districts, where it was reportedly used by Zheng-Dao Bioelectric's own security forces during a unionization dispute four years ago. Footage of workers convulsing on a factory floor circulated widely and permanently damaged Zheng-Dao's public image. The company has since pivoted aggressively to medical applications of the same technology, marketing axonal stimulation devices for nerve regeneration therapy — a rebranding effort that has been met with open mockery in affected communities. The weapon is called 'The Puller' in some neighborhoods as a reference to the way it seems to pull the body apart from the inside.
story_hooks: A mid-level Zheng-Dao executive has been found dead with neurological damage consistent with ASRL-3 exposure — but the weapon was never recovered, and the official cause of death is listed as a degenerative nerve condition. Someone with access to the weapon and the medical knowledge to disguise the damage killed this person very carefully.

A street medic in the labor district has been quietly documenting cases of permanent nerve damage in workers who were never officially reported as injured. She believes Zheng-Dao used the ASRL-3 on people and then paid for their silence with company medical coverage. She needs someone to help her get the evidence out.

The party is hired to retrieve a stolen ASRL-3 prototype with a modified frequency range that can affect myelinated axons in the central nervous system — which standard models cannot reach. If that calibration data gets out, someone could build a weapon that causes brain damage at range.
